items.question: Why do you favor co-designing product and research as Reflection AI’s approach to building superintelligence?
items.object: Co-designing product and research to build superintelligence at Reflection AI
items.answer:
I think there are different ways of thinking about how to build superintelligence and what that might look like. On one spectrum there's an academic way to look at it, which is, to some extent, superintelligence in that sense has already been achieved. AlphaGo was a superintelligent system, and there were other systems during that time that were built that were superintelligent in narrow domains. You can go for the goal of building a very broad superintelligence by locking yourself up in an industrial lab that is sort of decoupled from product or customers, and maps out all the benchmarks that are out there, and build superintelligence that way. I think that is one approach.

I think the other approach is to think about what superintelligence is more concretely. How is it going to be deployed? What is it actually going to look like in people's hands? Build backwards from there. I would say that approach is more co-designing product and research together. The benefits of that approach are that you're optimizing for real problems. The cons are that you have to be a lot more focused, right? Because your product defines the capabilities that you want to draw out of the system, and you have to start out a lot more focused before expanding across other product categories and other capabilities.

On the spectrum of companies that are just a research lab and then figure out what the product is once it's built, as opposed to co-designing product and research together to build very powerful systems in what I would call ASI-complete categories, you can pick something that's maybe too small of a category to draw out a superintelligence. As long as you pick a category that I would say is big enough to be ASI-complete, I think—and this is our approach at Reflection—it makes a lot more sense to be focused and co-design those two things together, the product and the research.

items.question: Why did you see physics as the root science to pursue?
items.object: Physics as a root science
items.answer: Physics was so interesting because it seemed like the science that was at the root of many of the things that became impactful. I was reading about the history of the transistor, and it was invented by a group of theoretical physicists. I was reading about how GPS works. It turns out you need special relativity in order to accurately account for spatial coordinates using GPS. I felt that physics was the root science to pursue.

It turns out you need special relativity in order to accurately account for spatial coordinates using GPS. I felt that physics was the root science to pursue.

items.question: Why did you come to see AI as the science to bet on?
items.object: AI as the root science of its time
items.answer:
I started seeing deep learning take off and saw AlphaGo happen. My sense was that I wanted to pursue the root science, but there is such a thing as the root science of our time. I think a lot of physics is a field that's very interesting, but it's crystallized a lot more than a new dynamic field that was being born out of nothing. AI to me felt like it was going through the moment that physics went through maybe a hundred years ago. When I did problem sets in physics, the most exciting stuff that I was working on there was basically the things that people were discovering 100 years ago. So I saw it happening in front of my eyes, and I decided that that was the science to bet on.

In particular, it was AlphaGo that inspired me, because it was just unbelievable to me that you could train a neural network to have such immense, basically reasoning capabilities. This thing was superintelligent within the realm of Go. I decided that I needed to get myself into the best reinforcement learning lab I could, and Peter's lab was that lab for me.

items.question: How did your experience working on Gemini 1.5 shape your view of scaling reinforcement learning on top of large language models?
items.object: Scaling reinforcement learning on top of large language models
items.answer: It was a really exciting time because we went, both of us, from being reinforcement learning researchers to training large language models at scale. We saw at the end of that project what was to come, which was Gemini 1.5 landing, and it became pretty clear to us that the next paradigm, and effectively the final paradigm we need to have in place before what people used to call AGI, or now I think the goalposts have shifted to ASI, is reached, is figuring out how to scale reinforcement learning on top of large language models. The first instances of that have been happening over the last year. I think we're still actually a lot earlier than people think, but there's a weathervane and things have started to work.

items.question: How do you see Asimov’s role among AI coding tools for enterprises?
items.object: Asimov’s role among enterprise AI coding tools
items.answer:
So Asimov is the best code research agent in the world. It's a comprehension agent, meaning that it's really designed to feel almost like deep research for large codebases. The way a developer is supposed to feel interacting with it is effectively like they have a principal-level engineer who deeply understands their organization at their fingertips.

It's very different from the existing set of tools that are focused primarily on code generation. Every single coding tool has some code generation and some comprehension aspect. But as we spent a lot of time with our customers trying to understand why coding tools—and this is enterprise-specific, so I think the world is different with startups—but within enterprises, when they're adopting coding tools and you see the impact this is having on their actual productivity, I think it's much lower than people expect. Sometimes it's negative, sometimes negligible.

items.question: How do you think AI tools should handle the knowledge scattered across a complex engineering organization?
items.object: Organizational understanding in AI engineering tools
items.answer:
The METR report was very close to what I've been hearing when talking to engineering leaders within larger organizations. And it's not just enterprises; it's growth-stage startups. It's any kind of engineering organization that has a sufficiently complex codebase and sufficiently large team that no one engineer can have the entire codebase in their heads.

Reflection is one of those places as well. We use our product actively because training large language models is complex. There's the large language model codebase, there's the product codebase; knowledge is scattered across engineers. It's not just in the codebase; it exists in your chats and project management tools and other places where knowledge lives. What we're effectively building towards is this omniscient oracle for organizations that you can go in and ask any question at any level of complexity, and it'll provide you an answer at the level of what that principal-level engineer would have given you—or, in the future, as the product expands to other categories, what the person who's most embedded in the organization understands.

items.question: Why do you think understanding deserves more emphasis than action in AI agents for engineering organizations?
items.object: Understanding versus action in engineering agents
items.answer: Once you have that solved, it begets much more reliable agents that act for you as well. But I think the world today is focused on, I would say, 80% action, 20% understanding: 80% code generation, 20% comprehension. The actual problem is exactly the opposite. When you look at what an engineer does in an organization, 80% of their time they're spending trying to comprehend complex systems and collaborating with teammates. And what is collaboration? It's usually someone asking someone else a question about a system that they don't know. That, I think, is the problem at the heart of what would prevent a superintelligence from actually working within an organization. It's this understanding and being able to ingest from a lot of sources of information and from the team. Once you have that, then the action part becomes a lot easier. To me, it seems like really 20% of the problem is teaching these agents how to act, and it's more or less solved.

items.question: Why do you think co-designing research and product is important for Asimov's ability to understand an engineering organization?
items.object: Co-designing research and product for Asimov's understanding of engineering organizations
items.answer:
I think this is where it is so important to co-design research and product, because as a researcher you'd go in and say the answer is entirely in the agent design or the model, and as a product person you would say, well, it's in these product differentiators, like being able to draw not just from your codebase but knowledge that lives in other sources of information, or being able to learn from the engineering team to offload their tribal knowledge.

An engineer can go in and teach it, like, “Hey, when we say environment jobs on our team, we mean this specific thing, which we mean Google Batch jobs.” So now when another engineer asks a question about environment jobs in the future, the system just knows what they're talking about. A lot of knowledge is stored in engineers' heads. I think you need both of these things. You need to understand your customer really closely and develop differentiated product almost independently of the models that are powering it. But then you also need to innovate on the research in terms of agent design and model training to drive the capabilities that you want to see out of the system.

items.question: How important do you think evaluations are to the capabilities that distinguish frontier AI models?
items.object: Evaluation as a source of frontier model capability
items.answer: This becomes an evaluation problem, which is basically at the heart of any frontier lab as well. This is the least spoken-about part of what frontier labs do, but possibly the most important, which is figuring out how they evaluate. What makes Claude magically feel better at code than another model out there? They did something right in their evaluations.

items.question: How do you approach training the capabilities an AI agent needs to be useful to end users?
items.object: Training agent capabilities for end-user usefulness
items.answer:
When you look at this problem specifically, there are different capabilities that you need to train, and what we do is we really post-train models. We really focus on post-training today. Some of these things are long-context reasoning. When I say long-context reasoning, I actually mean small models with very long contexts that are able to go into giant codebases, suck up as much information as they can, reason over it, and output relevant stuff. It's almost like neural retrieval.

There are capabilities like tool use and multihop reasoning. This is more for when you have your agent and it's designed with some tools. There are two ways of training agentic models. One is in this very general way, where you train it on thousands of environments and make it the most general agent possible. That's kind of almost like the pre-training of agents, and that's what a frontier lab does. That's what this new release from Kimi 2 does. That's definitely part of it, but that kind of gives you a nice general base to start from.

But then to drive a capability depth-wise, if you really want this reasoner that has search tools and the ability to call these long-reasoning-context models and other tools it might want to interact with—when do I read from Jira, when do I read from another tool?—this is a reasoning problem. If you train with those specific tools in mind, that's typically what people refer to when they say tool use: they actually train for a specific set of tools and really drive the capabilities for those tools.

These are the kinds of research problems that you need to solve in order to build the overall system that's the best in the world. It's not any one thing; it's all these things combined. An example of systems trained for a specific set of tools is Grok 4. They showed a plot of their general model and then the model that was trained with a tool to basically climb on Humanity's Last Exam, and there was some big noticeable difference between the two. That's great, but does Humanity's Last Exam actually matter in any meaningful way for an end user? I would argue some weak correlation, but the answer is most likely no. You have to build the tools and train for the things that users actually want. I think there's sort of no way around that.

items.question: How do you think a coding AI startup can compete with incumbent labs that have billions of dollars to pre-train models?
items.object: A coding AI startup's competitive advantage over incumbent model labs
items.answer:
The only advantage that you'll ever have as a startup over a big incumbent, especially when there are such talented teams out there, is focus and velocity against the thing that you're focused on. If you want to be playing in what is arguably the biggest category in AI, which is coding, then you need the talent as well to do it. But what do you do if you don't have the billions of dollars to pre-train models? The only way we can win, I think, is by being very focused.

The way I would describe what it looks like to work on a big model within an incumbent lab is that you are one of hundreds of evals. When you look at the model card for, let's say, the o1 paper that came out last year, if you look at the distribution of what most people work on in that paper, it was evals. You're one of many people doing all sorts of evals and spreading yourself; in that sense, you get something that's general, but it's spread fairly thin.

items.question: How do you translate customer needs into evaluations that improve Asimov's performance?
items.object: Customer-driven evaluation and system development for Asimov
items.answer:
As a startup with a very focused product that's not being too diffused and is pretty opinionated about what it's building, your evals are basically what, in the startup lore, Paul Graham would tell you: go talk to customers. Half the time build product, half the time talk to customers. I think in the AI age it's develop your evals based on what customers are saying and what they're doing. You have to work with your customers to look at what prompts they're trying to solve, what general questions they're trying to unlock. There are very specific pain points we've identified, like onboarding. In a big company it takes months to onboard an engineer. How do you develop evals that accelerate onboarding an engineer from months to hopefully just a couple of weeks, now that all the questions they had they can just ask Asimov and be able to onboard much faster?

There's no silver bullet other than coupling to the information coming from customers, but then being very scientific in the evals that you develop across them. You have customer needs, let's say onboarding and a bunch of others, and then you have your system capabilities. What do you need in order to provide a good experience there? This customer is being onboarded onto a giant codebase; it might be a codebase that's on its own 100 million tokens or something. Then you need to figure out some way to reason over that giant codebase, so you have a long-context reasoning capability, or you look at your agent and see what's preventing it from satisfying this query from a user. You work backwards and reverse-engineer from what a user is asking for to what capabilities you want to drive in your system.

The important part is to be able to tweak every part of the system, from the product features to the agent design to the model training, in order to build the best overall system. If you're capped in which parts you can change—if you can only change the product and agent design—then you're pretty limited, because you're at the mercy of what these general third-party models can do.

items.question: Where do you think your deep research-style coding assistant provides the most value for engineers?
items.object: Semantic queries as a use case for a deep research-style coding assistant
items.answer:
I think the kinds of queries that it tends to be better at are what we would call semantic queries. An example of a query where this is not the best system to use is file-level. If you're looking at a file and there's a specific thing in that file and you're just trying to get a quick answer to it, you don't need the hammer of a deep research-like experience. You don't need to wait tens of seconds or a minute or two to get that answer, because that should just be delivered snappily.

But if you don't exactly know where you're looking, you don't know the function name or something, and this is kind of the hard problem that engineers are usually in—like there's a flaky test. You know that this test is flaky, but that's where your knowledge stops. That's when you usually go to Slack and ask an engineer, “This test is flaky. What's going on? Does anyone know?”

The way we've used it is, when you're training these models, there's a lot of infrastructure work that goes into it, and it fails in interesting ways all the time. Asking things like, “My jobs are running slowly, five times more slowly than usual. Why is that?” is a vague query that would be very hard to answer with existing systems, especially since the knowledge around that query might live not just in the codebase. In the example I just brought up, when our environment jobs were slowing down, it turned out that two different teams, infrastructure and research, submitted pull requests that passed tests. It wasn't that they were wrong, but they conflicted together in a way that caused effectively a race condition and slowed everyone's jobs down. These are the kinds of bugs that engineers spend a few days trying to solve, with two or three engineers.

I think these kinds of semantic queries tend to be the place where a product like this shines. In the same way that, when you think of what kind of query you'd ask ChatGPT to use the browser tool for, a quick factual thing, you wouldn't invoke the deep research experience. But when you wanted to compile a lot of information around some more nebulous query, that's where people seem to find a lot of value with deep research. I think a similar mindset holds here.

items.question: How do you think about designing shared team memory that helps language models understand a codebase?
items.object: Shared team memory that helps language models understand codebases
items.answer: The way it's worked with customers we've started working with is they typically want to start off with a group of trusted senior staff-plus engineers who are the gatekeepers, which is a very common notion. You have permissions and ownership structure in codebases, and they basically are the ones who populate the memory first and then expand the scope. I think it works. It's actually a much more complex feature to build because it touches on wide permissions. There are some parts of the code where a certain engineer should be able to edit the memory but other engineers shouldn't. It starts looking like the new way of versioning code, effectively. It's kind of GitHub++, because you're not versioning the code, you're versioning the meta-knowledge around it that helps language models understand it better. Definitely that is something that we built, but I think it's a thing to iterate a lot until you get the right design here, because you're effectively building a new Git from scratch.

items.question: How did you think about the opportunity for Reflection AI to build competitive coding systems using open-weight models and reinforcement learning without paying for pre-training up front?
items.object: Reflection AI's decision to build on open-weight models and focus on reinforcement learning
items.answer:
I think that's roughly correct for why you can get into the game short-term. A bet that we made when we were starting a company a year and a half ago was that there were pretty decent open-weight models out there. We kind of saw pre-training as starting to more or less converge on a known paradigm. There's a known big data set on the internet. Yes, there are going to be some algorithmic innovations, but you're basically extracting signal from an extremely noisy data set. We felt like there's only so much signal that one would be able to extract without getting into absurd dollars for scaling this, in terms of what you're trying to get out of it.

We thought there'd be decent open-weight models. I think the quality of the open-weight frontier has surprised me. The models are better than I thought they would be, and we thought that you can just focus on—we're in this brief period in history right now where the RL flops are still manageable. You can really have a best-in-class product if you're focused. Yes, you'll need to put a decent amount of GPUs, but from a flops perspective it's nowhere near where pre-training is, like two magnitudes off.

items.question: Why do you see rewards as the fundamental bottleneck to scaling reinforcement learning?
items.object: Reward availability as a bottleneck to scaling reinforcement learning
items.answer:
I'd say that there are two categories, or one would think that things fall into: one is more around the problem limitations of the problem structure, and the other one is, well, maybe the structure is fine but you need algorithmic advances to really drive the next frontier forward. There's some mixture of both, but the biggest way I put it is on the problem structure.

The thing that I led for Gemini was reward models. I built out the reward models that were used to post-train Gemini 1.5. I thought that if you have a reward that accurately describes the outcome of any arbitrary task that you throw at it, then that's it. At that point it's just algorithmic advances. Even the very simple RL methods we have today will be able to get a lot out of this; they'll only be bound by their exploration abilities. But today we certainly are not in this world where we have clean rewards for every task we could imagine, and so as a field we have to make various shortcuts and compromises.

You'll have things like LLM-as-judge with different rubrics, and that works to some extent, but a noisy or stochastic reward inevitably gets hacked. You need a lot of these, and there's only so much you can extract out of them. Then you have sources that do have ground-truth rewards, but there are not many of them, and so you have to hope that by optimizing against those you'll get some generalization effects. I think the fundamental problem is the reward problem. You can either say, “I'm just going to focus on rewards,” or, “I'm going to take things as they are and just be more creative in the methods that leverage the rewards that have them today.” Examples of that are basically every synthetic-generation pipeline. It's a messy problem, but I think fundamentally we're in a reward-bound world.

I don't think there's going to be any breakthrough where all of a sudden we go from not having rewards for everything to having them, because the reward problem in itself is—at the time I called it AGI-complete, now I'd say it's ASI-complete. By the time you have a neural network that can accurately verify any outcome, that is probably a superintelligence. It goes back to evaluations: what if you're training your reward models on something? What are you evaluating against? What are the tasks you want it to be good at? That's how I think about it. It's a fundamentally reward-model- or rewards-bound field.

items.question: What do you see as the algorithmic weaknesses of current reinforcement learning methods?
items.object: Exploration and credit assignment in current reinforcement learning algorithms
items.answer: The RL methods we have today are quite bad, I would say, at exploration and credit assignment. The fundamental algorithms are: take the things that work and make them happen more frequently, and the things that don't work and make them happen less frequently. But they don't discern along your reasoning chain which part of the reasoning was correct and which part was incorrect. That's why you get these reasoning chains that are garden-path, meandering. They'll explore all sorts of things that are completely unnecessary and don't look at all like the kind of structured thinking that a person would have. That's how the algorithm works. It doesn't actually look at—there's no credit-assignment step on any atomic level. That falls into more algorithmic-progress bottlenecks.

items.question: Why would you consider the problem of artificial superintelligence solved once superintelligent systems exist in particular categories?
items.object: Solving artificial superintelligence as a technical versus economic problem
items.answer:
The reason why I would say that the problem of ASI would have been solved is because at that point it's just a matter of operationalizing. It just so happened that these particular categories—you might have a superintelligent front-end developer because there's so much data distribution for that on the internet, and it's easier to make synthetic data for that. At that point, you have the recipe, and it's just a matter of making economic decisions: is it worth sinking in X amount of dollars to get the data in this category to get something close to superintelligence there?

An example is what happened with reinforcement learning before language models. The blueprint for building superintelligent systems was developed. It happened with the Atari games, AlphaGo, then Dota 5 and AlphaStar were near-superintelligent systems. If OpenAI and DeepMind had sunk more compute into them, they would have definitely become superintelligent. It's just that at that point it didn't make economic sense. Why would you do that?

items.question: How do you assess frontier AI labs' ability to turn their models into successful coding products through vertical integration?
items.object: Frontier AI labs vertically integrating into coding products
items.answer:
Coding has clearly become one of these categories where verticalization is extremely important. On the frontier lab side, this is exactly what Giannis and I noticed when we were working in Gemini: your model is so far away from the product that oftentimes, even though you have the best model, that does not at all mean that you have the best product. There's a reason why startups are the places where adoption of coding tools took off rather than the frontier labs. There's a verticalization happening there. Some are going to do it successfully and some are not. We're already starting to see that with Claude Code really being an example of successful verticalization.

I don't think it's guaranteed that a big lab can buy its way to the end user, because the fundamental problems of your research team being far away from your product team will still be true, and the company having a hundred different focus areas will still be true. I don't think that acquiring an asset will change that fundamentally, but it does underscore the importance of verticalization.

items.question: How do you view the competitive position of search and coding startups that depend on another company's frontier models?
items.object: Search and coding startups that depend on other companies' frontier models
items.answer:
From the startup side, I think it puts companies that are in critical-path categories like search and coding in a pretty existential place if they can't build their own frontier models. Not all frontier labs will be able to verticalize correctly, but some will. Maybe one will, and that's going to be enough to take the thunder out from a company that's built a great user experience on top of someone else's model. There are some question marks if you're in a critical-path category and don't have your own intelligence: how do you compete when your competitor can subsidize their product a lot more than you can?

As a startup building on top of these things to grow quickly, you're subsidizing the margin that an Anthropic or Gemini or whatever is making, and Google and Anthropic and OpenAI can subsidize their products a lot more than you can. Companies that don't own their intelligence or aren't deeply integrated into a customer in some way that makes them hard to remove find themselves in this existential place as it becomes clear to the frontier labs that this is a category they need to verticalize around.

items.question: Why do you see reward signals as a fundamental bottleneck for reinforcement learning in robotics?
items.object: Reward signals as a bottleneck for reinforcement learning in robotics
items.answer:
I was actually a robotics researcher in reinforcement learning in Peter Abbeel's lab. It was a mixture: Peter's lab was always around the intelligence problem, and robotics was a domain where you study it. One reason I came to lead reward models for Gemini was because that's the question I was studying with robotics. We had these RL algorithms for getting robots to do very narrow tasks, like moving blocks and various narrow tasks in simulation. The question was, how do we get generalized manipulators, and how do we build this all into one system? It seemed like the rewards were the bottleneck.

A lot of what I was studying before getting into language models was how do we design reward functions or models for robotics or for 3D video games like Minecraft that have similar challenges scientifically. If you think language-model rewards are hackable, vision-language-model rewards or other sensory-signal rewards are infinitely more hackable. You can think of language as just a compressed representation of the world that we magically have to start with. Whereas if you're processing pixels or sensory-motor signal, this is raw signal that has a lot more noise in it. If you train a neural network that's trying to detect whether this thing was manipulated correctly or moved correctly, that thing is infinitely more hackable than anything you have in language models. The same problems blow up and become much larger.

That's why I changed to language models, because I felt this was a fundamental problem, but we now have these confounding factors of noisy signals coming in. In a generalizable way, that's why it's really hard to get reinforcement learning to work with robotics. The one place where it really does work well is when you have a clean reward signal, which happens to be in locomotion scenarios. There's a lot of work on building very robust sim-to-real locomotion pipelines, because locomotion is just your body; you don't have to manipulate the world around you. You can build reward signals like, “Your quadruped is moving at this velocity without damaging its body.”

items.question: Why do you think language models favor synthetic data and reinforcement learning compared with robotics?
items.object: Imitation learning versus synthetic data and reinforcement learning for language models
items.answer:
These two fields are very different in the data distributions they support. The imitation-learning data for language models is the internet. People have gathered all this data on how we write and so forth. Aside from that, when we're generating synthetic data, the only scalable path is really reinforcement learning.

The other thing I'll say is that when you're collecting data for robotics, you can do it in this teleop way. These are things that we're trying to train robots to do that are very intuitive for humans as well—actually more intuitive for humans. People are master manipulators, so you can have a lot of teleop-like data collection. The things that we want language models to do are at the level where it's really hard to collect data of the chain-of-thought process that goes on in a human's head when they're trying to solve some task. That's the data you need, and for that reason I think language models favor this more synthetic-data, RL-like approach, where it's easier for us to verify whether the thing was done or not than to actually generate all that data from a person.

The other thing I'll say is that when you're collecting data for robotics, you can do it in this teleop way. These are things that we're trying to train robots to do that are very intuitive for humans as well—actually more intuitive for humans. People are master manipulators, so you can have a lot of teleop-like data collection. The things that we want language models to do are at the level where it's really hard to collect data of the chain-of-thought process that goes on in a human's head when they're trying to solve some task. That's the data you need, and for that reason I think language models favor this more synthetic-data, RL-like approach, where it's easier for us to verify whether the thing was done or not than to actually generate all that data from a person.

The response explains that human internal reasoning is harder to collect as demonstration data for language models than human manipulation is to collect through teleoperation for robotics.
The response states that verifying successful completion of a language-model task is easier than collecting a human's reasoning process for solving it.

items.question: Why do you see coding as a foundation for AI systems that can work beyond software engineering?
items.object: Coding as a foundation for AI systems across categories of work
items.answer: The thing that makes coding as a category special is that it's not synonymous with software engineering. That's just how we think about the market today. The reason code is special is if you believe that the way a language model will interact with almost any piece of software is through function calls and therefore code, then if you build very capable reasoning coding reasoners that are purpose-built for an organization—so you've solved the long-context, how-do-I-reason-over-a-bunch-of-information-from-disparate-sources problem, and I can act on pieces of software through code—then you've built a system, the technology that will generalize, at least operationally, across other categories of work.

items.question: How do you think Reflection should approach expanding beyond software engineering?
items.object: Reflection's strategy for expanding beyond software engineering
items.answer: The way I think about it is, first just build—not trying to get too ahead of yourself—the most depth-wise comprehension system for software engineers. This will naturally induce more reliable coding agents. You can plug that in as an MCP to your favorite IDE or coding agent, or use one of our own. You can plug that into whatever surface area makes sense for the customer and then naturally start seeing where you're getting pulled from there. The reason I think this will work is because this is what we're already seeing: how do you make the system useful for product managers or technical support people, and then moving on to things like sales? There are already places where customers are pulling us in different directions. It's a matter of whether you engage on that today or not. The risk a startup has is that you see a lot of shiny areas where you can go and start going diffuse before you've really nailed a category. I think it's really important to be focused and not diffused in the short term, and if you build the right—as we think about it—as a contextual core for an organization, in this case an engineering organization, then you can naturally start expanding that into adjacent areas of work in that enterprise.

items.question: How do you see the timeline for deploying superintelligence across different categories of work?
items.object: The timeline for deploying superintelligence across categories of work
items.answer: I think we're a lot earlier than most people think. This is going to be one of those areas where the technological building blocks outpace their deployment. Within the next couple of years, the blueprint roughly for how to build ASI will have been set, more or less. Maybe there are still some efficiency breakthroughs that need to happen, but more or less there will be a blueprint for how to build a superintelligence in a particular category. Actually going in and deploying it and building it for specific categories of work will require a lot of product and research innovation specific to those categories. That will probably make this a multi-decade thing. I don't think it's a couple of years from now and GDP starts growing 10% year-over-year globally. I think we're actually going to get there, but it's going to be a multi-decade endeavor.

items.question: Why do you expect AI companies focused deeply on particular categories of work to emerge?
items.object: Category-specific AI agents and depth-first AI companies
items.answer: I see a lot of patterns now in real-world deployment with reinforcement-learning research as it worked before large language models. Before large language models, you pick an environment, like Go, StarCraft, or something else, and try to solve it with some combination of imitation learning and reinforcement learning. When you look at all those projects, these were basically things that were called strikes within DeepMind. Each strike within and outside of DeepMind was a bit of a snowflake. The reinforcement-learning methods and environment setup for Go were conceptually similar at a high level, but at the detailed implementation level very different from StarCraft, very different from Dota 5. I think we're going into every big category having a different environment and different kinds of agents with different tools. That means you'll have general base models you can start with, but you'll need to post-train things in specific ways for those categories. We're starting to see that already: the model that powers OpenAI's Codex is not the O-series of models; it's a model called Codex, post-trained for that environment. The deep research models—that's a specific environment; they're also post-trained for that environment. I think we'll see more and more that any category with a sufficiently large business around it that requires an intelligence score to power it will have all sorts of interesting design decisions at the research and product level about how to gain the most performance out of that particular category. I think we'll see a lot more depth-first players emerge over the coming decade or so. I'm making a bet on it.

items.question: How do you see the timeline for AI coding to produce its next generation of major companies?
items.object: The timing of AI coding’s emergence as a major commercial category
items.answer: I think coding is this era as well. This one I think will take longer than people thought, because enterprise organizational problems are just much different than the benchmarks that we have today. But I think it will be one of the faster ones. I don't think that's a decade out; that's within the next dozen dozens of months kind of thing. The next generational companies in coding are definitely being built today.
